title: German troops cross into Belgium
summary: Belgium having refused passage, German cavalry and the Army of the Meuse cross the frontier near Gemmenich on the morning of 4 August and move on Liège. Britain's ultimatum expires that night.

title: Siege of Liège
summary: The coup de main of 5–6 August fails against the forts; Ludendorff takes the citadel on 7 August; the forts fall one by one to 42 cm and 30.5 cm howitzers between 12 and 16 August. The armies of the right wing begin their march on 18 August.

title: Battle of the Frontiers
summary: Plan XVII's offensive into Lorraine (14–20 August, Morhange–Sarrebourg) and the Ardennes (21–23 August) is thrown back with heavy losses, while on the Allied left the German right wing drives the French 5th Army from the Sambre at Charleroi (21–23 August) and meets the British at Mons (23 August). The general retreat follows.

title: The Belgian field army withdraws into Antwerp
summary: Ordered back from the Gette on the 18th as the German 1st Army came on, the field army is inside the national redoubt by the 20th; Brussels is occupied the same day. From now on the Belgian army is a threat on the flank of the German communications, and a corps is turned off the wheel to watch it.

title: The first sortie from Antwerp
summary: Four Belgian divisions come out towards Malines and Louvain to pull German strength back from the Sambre; they are stopped by the III Reserve Corps and go back when the news comes that the French and British are retreating. Louvain burns that night.

title: Louvain burned
summary: German troops in the university town, convinced they are under fire from civilians as units fall back from the Belgian sortie and others arrive at dusk, shoot some 248 inhabitants, burn about a sixth of the town and the university library with its manuscripts, and expel the population. With Dinant, Tamines and Aarschot it is the 'rape of Belgium' that shapes neutral opinion — and, a century on, the best-documented of the reprisals.

title: Joffre's Instruction générale no 2
summary: Joffre abandons Plan XVII: the armies will retreat, and a new mass of manoeuvre — the future 6th Army — will be formed on the left by rail from the Lorraine front, to strike the German right wing's outer flank.

title: Kluck wheels south-east, inside Paris
summary: Believing the French left beaten and anxious to keep touch with Bülow, Kluck turns the 1st Army south-east on 30–31 August to pass east of Paris — exposing his right flank to the garrison of Paris and the new 6th Army.

title: First Battle of the Marne
summary: Maunoury's 6th Army strikes Kluck's flank on the Ourcq; Kluck swings his corps back north-west to meet it, widening the gap between his army and Bülow's; the BEF and Franchet d'Espèrey's 5th Army advance into the gap; Foch holds at Saint-Gond. On 9 September, after Hentsch's visit, the 1st and 2nd Armies retreat.

title: Maubeuge surrenders
summary: After thirteen days of investment and nine of bombardment by the heavy howitzers brought on from Namur, Fournier surrenders the fortress and some forty thousand men; the VII Reserve Corps is free to march — a week after the Marne opened, and a day after the decision there had turned.

title: The second sortie from Antwerp
summary: Timed to the Marne: the field army comes out again towards Aarschot and Louvain, retakes Aarschot and puts its cavalry at the edge of Louvain before German reinforcements — a reserve division turned back north and a division from Alsace — press it back into the fortress on the 13th.

title: Retreat to the Aisne
summary: The German right wing falls back 60–80 km to the heights north of the Aisne and digs in; Moltke is replaced by Falkenhayn on 14 September. The mobile war in the West is over.

title: The armies dig in on the Aisne
summary: Attack after attack on the Chemin des Dames fails against troops who are below ground. Within a fortnight both sides have continuous trenches, wire and registered artillery, and the spade has beaten the boot: the way to make ground is no longer to march round a flank but to break through one — and nobody yet knows how.

title: The Ardennes: the French offensive stopped in a day
summary: The main effort of Plan XVII. The French 3rd and 4th Armies advanced into the Ardennes against what Joffre believed was a weak German centre and met two German armies moving the other way; after one day of encounter battles at Rossignol, Bertrix, Ethe and Virton they fell back to the Meuse.[^afgg-1-1] [^doughty-2005]

title: The race to the sea
summary: Four times in a month each side reaches north to get round the other's open flank — Picardy, the Santerre, Artois, Flanders — and four times both arrive at once and the line simply grows northward. It was never a race for the sea; it was a race for a flank, which the sea finally abolished.

title: The Second Army's attempt in Picardy
summary: Castelnau's Second Army, brought west out of Lorraine by rail, tries to work round the German right about Roye and Lassigny and meets German forces arriving by the same means. The first of the northward attempts stalls in a week.

title: The Tenth Army formed at Arras
summary: Joffre improvises a third northern army under de Maud'huy at Arras. It is met head-on by Rupprecht's Sixth Army, arriving from Lorraine; Arras is held, the German attempt to take it fails, and the line stops a few kilometres east of the city for four years.

title: Foch sent north as Joffre's deputy
summary: Joffre makes Foch his deputy for the northern armies, with the job of coordinating the French forces there and, as far as persuasion allows, the British and the Belgians too. It is the first Allied coordination of the war in the West, and it is done without any authority over the allies it coordinates.

title: Antwerp falls
summary: Beseler's siege train opens on the outer forts on 28 September and works through them as it had at Liège and Namur. A British naval brigade arrives on 4–6 October, too late and too light to change the arithmetic. The Belgian field army leaves westward on 6–8 October rather than be shut up with the city; Antwerp surrenders on 10 October, and some thirty thousand Belgian troops cross into the Netherlands and are interned for the duration.

title: The BEF moves from the Aisne to Flanders
summary: At Sir John French's request the BEF is taken out of the Aisne line by night, marched to the railheads and moved north by train to its own supply ports — a fortnight's work, carried out corps by corps and, for a time, concealed from the Germans. It arrives on the last open flank in Europe.

title: Lille occupied
summary: The German Sixth Army takes Lille after three days' bombardment. France's fifth city and the industry of the north pass under an occupation that lasts until October 1918.

title: The battle of the Yser
summary: The Belgian field army, six exhausted divisions with the sea at its back, holds the last twenty kilometres of unoccupied Belgium along the Yser embankment, with Ronarc'h's French marines at Dixmude. By the end of October it has been pushed off the far bank and is fighting on the railway embankment behind it.

title: The sea let in: the Yser inundation
summary: Belgian engineers, guided by men who worked the polders for a living, open the locks of the Ganzepoot at Nieuwpoort to the flood tide on a succession of nights, so that the sea runs inland faster than it can drain. By 30 October the water is four to five kilometres wide and rising, the German positions are islands, and the attack across the Yser stops for good. The front's northern anchor is not a fortress but a flood.

title: The First Battle of Ypres
summary: Falkenhayn's last attempt at a decision in 1914: the reconstituted Fourth Army and the Sixth attack the salient in front of Ypres for a month, in numbers the defenders cannot match. The line bends and holds, and the old British regular army is destroyed holding it.

title: The crisis at Gheluvelt
summary: The German attack breaks the line on the Menin road and takes Gheluvelt; for some hours the road to Ypres is open and the British divisional staffs are being shelled out of their headquarters. A single under-strength battalion counter-attacks across open ground into the village and retakes it. The salient holds because the reserve arrived before the breakthrough was noticed.

title: The Prussian Guard on the Menin road
summary: The last heavy German effort at Ypres: the Guard attacks astride the Menin road, breaks into the British line at Nonne Bosschen and is stopped by cooks, orderlies and engineers fed into the gap. After it the Flanders offensive is closed down.

title: The continuous front
summary: By the end of November the trenches run without a gap from Nieuwpoort on the North Sea to the Swiss frontier — some seven hundred kilometres with no flank to turn at either end. The war of movement that the plan was built to win in six weeks is over in four months, and the war it was built to avoid has begun.

title: Joffre relieves Ruffey
summary: Ruffey is removed from the 3rd Army and replaced by Sarrail — one of some fifty French general officers Joffre relieved in August and September. Ruffey argued to the end of his life that the two reserve divisions withheld from him for the Army of Lorraine had cost him the battle.[^doughty-2005]

sources.note: Joffre's relief of Ruffey on 30 August, Sarrail's succession, and the scale of the purge; Ruffey's own account of the withheld divisions is his, reported — not a finding

title: The Grand Couronné: Nancy holds
summary: Rupprecht's 6th Army attacks the heights covering Nancy for a week while the Marne is fought in the west. The position holds, and the two German armies in Lorraine spend the decisive week attacking entrenchments instead of reinforcing the wheel.[^afgg-1-1] [^herwig-2009]

title: Two corps are taken off the right wing for East Prussia
summary: With Namur fallen and the French in retreat everywhere, Moltke concludes that the West is won and East Prussia is not, and orders the Guard Reserve Corps and the XI Corps - with the 8th Cavalry Division - to entrain for the East. Nobody in East Prussia asked for them. They leave the wheel on 26 August, are on trains through the battle they were sent to fight, and are missing from the front on which the Marne is decided ten days later.[^herwig-2009] [^mombauer-2001]
